subject: physics
question_text: An ivory ball and a wet clay ball of the same size are dropped from the same height onto a hard floor. Which one rises higher after striking the floor, and why?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 9 Very Short Answer Question 15 (printed p.99). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: ivory has a Young's modulus far above wet clay's and behaves elastically over the impact, storing and returning the kinetic energy of the fall; wet clay is well past its elastic limit at ordinary impact forces and deforms permanently, so it returns almost none of that energy — the standard NCERT elastic-versus-plastic comparison.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Which ball rises higher
lines: Of the two, the ivory ball rises
higher after it strikes the floor.
The wet clay ball does not rebound;
it stays flattened where it lands.
steps.why: The height each ball rises to after impact is a direct measure of how much of its falling kinetic energy is returned to it rather than spent deforming the ball.
common_mistakes: Saying the clay ball rises higher because it is heavier. Weight does not decide the rebound; the material's elastic behaviour does.
Saying both balls rise to about the same height. Their rebound heights are very different.
steps.memory_tip: Ivory bounces back; wet clay stays where it lands.
steps.margin_note: Marked for naming the ivory ball as the one that rises higher, and that the clay ball does not rebound.

steps.label: The reason
lines: Ivory is highly elastic: it returns
almost all the stored energy as it
regains its shape, so it rebounds.
Wet clay is plastic: it deforms

lines.text: Elastic ivory rebounds; plastic clay does not

steps.why: An elastic body regains its original shape after the deforming force is removed and returns the energy stored during the deformation, while in a plastic body the kinetic energy is used up deforming it permanently and is given off mostly as heat, which is exactly why one ball bounces and the other does not.
common_mistakes: Naming only "ivory is harder" without using the words elastic and plastic, which are what the examiner is checking for.
Saying wet clay stores the energy of the fall. The kinetic energy is used up deforming the clay permanently and is given off mostly as heat, not stored for a rebound.
steps.memory_tip: Elastic returns to shape and gives the energy back; plastic uses up the energy in permanent deformation, given off as heat.
steps.margin_note: Marked for the words "elastic" and "plastic", tied to energy being returned or kept as permanent deformation.

insider_note: Full marks need both halves: naming the ivory ball AND explaining it with the words elastic and plastic, not just one.
